There isn’t a single way in which this game isn’t a mess. It’s a narrative mess, it’s a design mess, and its performance is selectively a mess. (I genuinely don’t know what in the Seven Hells my boy Gor Gor is cooking up in Wyrm’s Rock, but that place ran like a crippled snail.)

But I loved most of it.

I loved playing it and somehow interacting with an even more screwed-up version of D&D 5e’s mechanics, defying everything that is holy in game design, complete with its messy proficiency system and terrible class balance.

I loved the characters, even with the blatant favoritism.

I loved making my build and absolutely obliterating the game, even though most of the items sucked big tarrasque scrotum. It was genuinely funny watching late-game bosses fail to even take a turn before being sent straight to Hell. (I played on the game’s second-hardest difficulty, Tactician.)

The story also has some notable moments of excellence, which I won’t mention here.

Buy it. Play it. It gets a recommendation from me.

This is one of the best games I have ever played, period. Everything is masterfully done. The Developers thought of everything. Baldur's Gate 3 is honestly one of the best games of our generation, and should be in the discussion for greatest video game of all time.

An example of what you would wish for in a game. From an RPG perspective, an amazing storyline, loads of customisations from visuals to builds and memorable companions.  A game where choices matter!

A game that is not loaded with millions of microtransactions that prey on your fear of missing out or impulsiveness. A one-time purchase that was followed by many updates and improvements at no cost, and earned the well-deserved awards of Labour of Love and Game of the Year.

My advice is to take your time with this gem. This is not a game you should speed through or expect to finish in a few hours. Take your time and check out every nook and cranny, there is so much to explore. It took me approx. 120 to 150 hours on my first campaign due to leaving no stone unturned. Even after that, there is replayability, as different decision/moral paths taken will provide different story outcomes.

If it is your first time playing this kind of game, it might feel overwhelming at first. If that is the case, lower the difficulty, enjoy the story, as that is where the gold is. Save plenty and take the Honour mode difficulty on a repeat run, later!

With amazing mod support and the amount of mods made by the modding community, the game only gets better. Also don't forget the co-op multiplayer option, just don't expect the human-controlled custom "companions" to follow your ideal campaign script. Expect them to be more like sabotage buddies.

All in all, a game that I would recommend to any friend! 10/10, perfect experience! Well done, Larian, on this gem!

So here's an honest review from an RPGer to any D&D fans that expect this to be a masterclass RPG? Nope. As far as a TBS is concerned, this one is fair. It seems to me, lat least in the 1355 hours that I have played, that the game is crafted so that the statistics are about equal between the enemies and your toons at normal level, that is fine. 

What torques my jaw is that-if you choose to play on honor mode-not only do you not have the save handy, but the game just seems to me to give 10-15% statistical bonus to enemies and the same penalty to your toons. Go to honor mode? Probably 20-30% global bonuses and penalties. Not MORE enemies, or higher level enemies that you can see and go "Woah, hey-those guys are level 5" or whatever. No, you see "Lvl 2 Kuo toa" and it will miss once in 5 swings against your level 5 monk with AC 19 and Patient Defense running, while you try and attack their level 2 ass with AC 15 and you will hit about 1 in 5.

Some of you tough kids will say "Y U mad, bro? Play your skill level" and the point is-this ISN'T skill like this: it is foreknowledge of encounters and trying to stack your toon to max statistics and say "Fuck the D&D side of it!" I just kind of see it as lazy coding, but these guys started as TBS authors, so they're working their lane, I guess. Just thought some of you looking for an RPG might want to consider something cheaper if a D&D RPG game was your primary interest. Or at least, don't get worked up if your D&D gamer skills don't apply very well here. >.<

[h2]Honestly I went in fully expecting to hate this game from all the cult-like hype.[/h2]

I've played DnD here and enjoy turn based games so this sounded like coming home. What makes DnD memorable is the random bits of actions you can do to trip up the dungeon master. I genuinely think Baldur's Gate 3 is the first video game that captures that table top spirit with the amount of stuff you can do.

[b]The turn-based combat is crazy good[/b] where it's not just enemies taking turns trading stat checks, combat is treated like an actual playground where highground matters, lighting matters and environmental hazards matter. All coupled in with movement economy to manage around, surprisingly complex yet surprisingly simple.

The tabletop freedom extends way past combat where spells isn't nerfed for video game balance, speak with dead for example is quite paramount in opening separate narratives rather than useless voiceline fluff. Game lets fail going forwards as in a bad roll doesn't mean game over but forces you to adapt to the gamble you took as you would in actual DnD if the promised nat 20 was not so promised at all in a dire situation.

I initially played this on console a couple of years back but it's quite intoxicating playing it on PC, there's just nothing quite like it. Especially now that there's a huge workshop scene to extend the game further. However I will say it did take multiple sessions to get into it at the beginning. One of my favourite games, and one of those that set new standards for their genre. It might even be one of the best games up there.

The story is amazing, and the game is really complex (in the best way) and engaging. It constantly keeps you experimenting and thinking, and there's almost always more than one way to approach a situation.

The characters are exceptionally well written, with only a few exceptions. The voice acting is amazing, with outstanding performances across the whole cast.

Visually, the game is gorgeous. The art style is amazing and every place feels polished and fitting for the setting. Larian did again an amazing job.

The music ranges from good to very good. My problem is that I played Divinity: Original Sin 2, Larian's previous big game, and Baldur's Gate 3's music is heavily inspired by its soundtrack, which was better overall. I must admit I was a bit disappointed.

Another important thing to add: Larian delivered a fully finished game for the current standard price. Unlike most games nowadays, where studios rush releases and finish the content later (often releasing it as DLCs and charging for it!), Larian gives the the complete experience from the start.

Two small caveats: the game can be a bit overwhelming if you're new to the D&D rules, and a better tutorial on how they work would have helped me. I also would have liked more of a middle path between a "good" and an "evil" run. It feels like you're pushed a bit toward one extreme.

Story: 10/10
Music: 7/10
Characters: 10/10
Voice Acting: 10/10
Graphics and artstyle: 10/10

reviews.review: I have to admit, and I do not say this lightly, this game is an absolute masterpiece. In my nearly 20 years of gaming I have never EVER seen anything come remotely close to this in terms of pure love, effort and dedication. The amount of content you get for your money is absolutely mind blowing with very well over 150 hours required if you want to properly experience just one playthrough, and that's not accounting for the unbelievable replayability. Even the smallest, seemingly insignificant side quests have story relevance and multiple ways to go about completing them, everything is made with such painstaking attention to detail and a dynamic world in mind. The writing is utterly phenomenal, the characters believable, the voice actors just amazing and all this with people new to the world of D&D taken into consideration. Everything important is explained and shown to you in the world, with smaller tidbits of lore scattered in books around the environment, painting a complete picture of Faerun. And if that wasn't enough, the combat ties a perfect little bow on the whole thing, it's fun, it's challenging but fair, and rewards you thoroughly for using the environment and making smart choices, giving a true tactical sandbox experience. Overall, I have nothing but love for this game and I genuinely can not think of any way to improve it except to make that sequel. Thank you, Larian Studios, for the unforgettable experience!

Where do I even start with Baldur's Gate 3?

I've been playing D&D since I was around 11, so there was absolutely no way I was going to miss this game. I hadn't played the previous Baldur's Gate games, though, so BG3 was actually my introduction to the series. I got it as soon as it became available, and almost 1,000 hours later... apparently I'm still not done with it.

Achievements aren't really the focus for me here. I'm currently at 46/54, but BG3 is one of those games where I'd much rather start another character, try another choice and see where the story takes me than worry about completing a checklist.

The amount of freedom and variation is probably what I love most. Even after so many playthroughs, different interactions, consequences and unexpected outcomes can still appear. You make one seemingly insignificant choice differently and suddenly you're seeing something you've never seen before. It makes every run feel like its own D&D campaign rather than simply replaying the same story.

The modding possibilities make that experience even better. I love that the game can be modded so easily, although I've mostly kept mine to quality-of-life and graphical improvements. For me, it's about polishing and improving the experience without changing what makes the original game so good.

All three acts have something I love, although Act 2 is definitely my favourite. The atmosphere, the story and everything surrounding the Shadow-Cursed Lands just work incredibly well for me.

I love the companions too, although Gale, Astarion and Shadowheart have a special place among them. Gale takes first place when it comes to romance, though. ❤️

As for my own characters, Wizard is easily my favourite class and Drow my favourite race. Character creation gives you plenty to play around with, and combined with all the classes, subclasses, races, backgrounds, dialogue options and different ways of approaching situations, the replayability is enormous.

The story itself is great, but what really makes it special to me is how much it feels like *your* story. My most memorable Tav will probably always be my very first one, whom I played essentially as myself.

That adventure ended in Act 2 because I made a... let's call it a "wrong" decision.

The soundtrack deserves a mention as well. There are some beautiful tracks in there, and naturally, a few of them have found their way onto my Spotify playlists.

My main disappointment is knowing that development was, in some ways, rushed towards the end and that a number of things had to be cut. There are places where you can wonder what BG3 might have looked like if everything originally envisioned had made it into the finished game.

But even with that disappointment, what we got is still far more than excellent.

After 979.5 hours, countless characters, different decisions, romances, successes, catastrophes and apparently the occasional accidental premature ending, I'm still finding reasons to return to Baldur's Gate 3.

Best game I’ve played in years.

Honestly, the base game is just the tip of the iceberg. There’s already a ridiculous amount of content, freedom, different choices, builds, characters, and ways to play the game. You can finish a playthrough and start another one making completely different decisions, and it can feel like a totally different experience.

Then you get into the mods....

The modding community basically lets you turn Baldur’s Gate 3 into whatever you want it to be. New classes, subclasses, spells, weapons, armor, character customization, difficulty changes—you name it. If there’s something you wish the game had, there’s a good chance someone has made a mod for it.

After more than 350 hours in Baldur’s Gate 3, I can confidently say: this game is phenomenal.

What makes it so special is the freedom it gives you. You can talk your way through trouble, sneak past it, fight it head-on, or try something ridiculous and discover that the game actually allows it. Exploring different approaches is part of the fun, and the world’s reactions make your decisions feel meaningful.

The writing and performances deserve enormous praise. Characters have personality, conflicting motivations, and enough depth to make conversations worth paying attention to. Even smaller encounters can turn into memorable stories. There is so much care in the dialogue, environments, and little details that exploration feels rewarding beyond simply finding better equipment.

The combat is another highlight. Positioning, terrain, preparation, and the interaction between abilities give battles plenty of tactical depth. A clever plan can completely change an encounter, while a terrible plan can lead to something hilariously memorable. Experimenting with classes and builds adds another layer of enjoyment—and another reason to start a new character.

The replayability is incredible. Different choices, party compositions, and approaches give you reasons to revisit the adventure. This is a huge game, but its appeal goes beyond its size: it gives you room to make the experience your own.

It does ask for some patience. There are systems to learn, plenty of dialogue, and decisions that can keep you staring at the screen while you consider the possibilities. For me, that is a big part of the appeal. It is a game worth taking your time with.

More than 350 hours is probably the strongest recommendation I can give. Baldur’s Gate 3 combines tactical combat, fantastic storytelling, and an extraordinary amount of player freedom into something truly special.

Highly recommended. Just be careful with “one more quest.” That is rarely where the evening ends.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is an incredible game. The writing is engaging, the performances are fantastic, and the pacing feels nearly perfect. I’ve never been so completely immersed in a crafted world before. Great game. Love the mechanics. When playing Baldur's Gate 1 & 2, there was nothing about either one that indicated you were playing a D&D based game. Not so with Baldor's Gate 3.

Played both Divinity games so have experience with these type of Larian games. Those games were complex, but BG3 dials it up with an absurd amount of RNG. I'm no stranger to turn-based rpgs, but not super familiar with the DnD rule set. So I guess it appeals to the randomness of the tabletop. But from an actual RPG gameplay experience, I find all the extra RNG extremely tedious. So much so that the game, unfortunately, feels like a crawl to play. Setting/story draws you in well, but this game will trigger anyone with analysis paralysis. That's why this ~20 hr review is what it is. Initial impressions of the game are not great and the game doesn't seem warranted of it's crazy run time so far. However, I am willing to go back here and there and see if my experience improves. If things click better, perhaps i'll update my review. Clearly this game has an audience, just maybe not for me.

FINAL THOUGHTS: put in another 10+ hours, think i'm spent. The game is beautifully put together, it's just a shame that the actual gameplay/mechanics are so subpar. Even down right bad in areas. Maybe it's because I've played my fair share of other RPG/CRPGs, maybe it's just that I don't gel with the DnD ruleset present, but there isn't really anything that revolutionary here that hasn't been done in other games. Overall wanted more RPG, less RNG.
